title: Keep the student in the conversation
summary: Make room for preferences, communication, and dignity when the adults have a great deal to discuss.

Interests do not have to sound academic to matter to the person. Avoid reducing a teenager or adult student to a developmental-age comparison. Describe the specific assistance needed instead: support to make choices, help with transitions, accessible communication, or assistance with a daily activity. This keeps support needs visible while respecting the student's actual age and history. When a personal-care issue affects school participation, identify the educational question and the people who need the details. Dignity includes thoughtful limits on who hears sensitive information. Distinguish expression from interpretation+A useful note has three parts: what happened, the conditions around it, and what you think it may mean. For example: “When offered these two activities on three recent occasions, the student reached toward the music materials. We would like to understand whether this preference appears at school as well.” This is an illustrative observation, not a universal method for determining choice. It leaves room for the student to respond differently in another context. It also avoids turning an adult's interpretation into an unquestionable statement of the student's wishes. Include how much support was provided and who observed the response. If adults disagree about what a response means, name the uncertainty and ask what information or professional input would help. Avoid treating limited speech as evidence that the person has no preferences or nothing to contribute. Ask about communication across an ordinary day+Choose a few moments to explore with the Team: arrival, shared activities, a break, lunch, or dismissal. Ask how the student can express a choice, seek help, refuse, or indicate that something needs to change in each setting. Questions might include: What ways of communicating are recognized across staff and activities?What supports or equipment need to be available, and who checks that they are?How do staff allow time for a response and record the assistance used?What happens when familiar communication support is unavailable?How are new staff or substitutes prepared to follow the student's plan? These are educational planning questions to individualize with the Team. They are not a prescription for a particular communication system or treatment. Federal IDEA requires consideration of communication needs and whether assistive technology devices and services are needed. Read the special-factors provision. Plan participation that is useful to the student+Discuss whether and how the student will participate in the meeting, taking account of applicable requirements, their preferences, communication access, and support needs. Federal IDEA includes the student on the IEP Team whenever appropriate. When a meeting will consider postsecondary goals and the transition services needed to reach them, the agency must invite the student. If the student does not attend, the agency must take other steps to consider their preferences and interests. Read the participation and transition provisions. Participation might include joining a portion of a discussion or sharing an appropriately supported contribution prepared in advance. Do not assume those possibilities replace any requirement that applies to the particular meeting. Ask the Team how the student's perspective will be included and who will support access. As adulthood approaches, clarify the applicable state rules about educational decision-making rights. Family involvement does not automatically establish decision-making authority after rights transfer. Read IDEA's age-of-majority provision. Avoid requiring a polished performance to demonstrate that a preference matters. The purpose is to make the educational discussion more responsive to the person whose day it will shape. Bring the conversation back to daily life+Before moving on from a proposed support, ask: “What will this look like during an ordinary school day?” Then ask how the Team will know whether it is helping the student access learning and participate. Keep a short record of what is known, what was inferred, and what the Team agreed to explore. That modest habit protects both dignity and accuracy. It makes space for substantial support needs and an individual life in the same conversation. Educational information and practical organization ideas, not legal advice. Add one sentence about an interest, preference, or recent success that matters to the student. Avoid a catalogue of personal details. Share what helps the Team understand educational needs and participation. Then write your purpose in one sentence: “I would like us to understand how communication support is working across the day and decide what information or changes are needed.” This is an illustrative example, not a recommended goal for every student. Federal IDEA includes parents as IEP Team members and requires consideration of parent concerns in developing the IEP. Bringing an agenda is one practical way to organize that contribution. The Team still needs to work through the individual student's needs and the evidence. Team membership and IEP development. Copy this working template+Use the prompts below in a document you keep privately. Replace the brackets before sharing it with the appropriate school team. Our meeting Student: [name]Date and purpose: [meeting information]Something important to know: [interest, preference, strength, or meaningful success]What I hope we can accomplish: [one sentence] My three priorities Topic: [specific part of the school day or educational need]. What I have noticed: [brief observation and date]. My question or request: [what you want discussed].Topic: [second priority]. Relevant information: [report, example, or missing information]. My question or request: [specific next step to consider].Topic: [third priority]. Why it matters: [effect on access, participation, learning, or dignity]. My question or request: [specific discussion]. Before we finish What has been decided, and where will it be documented?What remains unresolved or requires more information?Who will do each next step, and what date has been agreed?What documents should I expect, and who should I contact with questions? Make each request easy to recognize+“Communication” is a subject. “Can we review how the student can make a choice during arrival, class activities, lunch, and dismissal?” gives the Team something concrete to answer. Likewise, “More data” can become: “Please explain what was counted, during which activities, and with what level of assistance.” You are asking to understand the information, rather than assuming that a percentage has a single obvious meaning. Separate your observation from your interpretation. “The report lists three opportunities” is an observation. “There may be too few opportunities to practice” is a question to explore. Both can belong on the page when the distinction is clear. Use the page during the conversation+Send the agenda ahead if that is practical. At the meeting, ask to identify where the priorities fit into the proposed discussion. Keep your own copy visible and mark an item as discussed, answered, or still open. Those are different things. If someone offers an answer that you do not understand, write a question mark rather than pretending it is settled. If time runs short, read the remaining requests aloud and ask how they will be handled. Avoid packing a major concern into an unexplained last-minute attachment. Afterward, use your marked agenda to prepare a short follow-up note. Save the original and your notes separately so you can tell what you planned to ask from what you actually heard. A useful agenda earns its place by making the next conversation easier, too. Educational information and practical organization ideas, not legal advice. Preserve documents about consent, acceptance, rejection, or other responses rather than relying on your memory of what was signed. If the status is unclear, ask the school to identify it; do not decide based solely on a filename. A small “to review” folder is useful because real life does not always leave time to file things perfectly. Emptying it once before a meeting is enough to make it valuable. Name files so you can recognize them later+Use date, document type, and a short description. For example: “2026-09-15_progress-report_communication.pdf.” Keep the original if you make a highlighted working copy, and add “working-notes” to the copy's name. For scanned pages, check that every page is present, upright, and readable. Make sure both sides were captured where needed. Searchable text is convenient, but inspect important names, dates, and numbers because automated text recognition can make mistakes. Do not put unnecessary identifying information into filenames that may appear in shared screens, notifications, or download lists. Use the level of detail you need within your own private system. Add an index before adding more technology+Keep a simple list with the document date, title, where it lives, and why it matters. One line per item is enough. An entry might say: “September progress report; Progress folder; ask how assistance was recorded.” This index is especially helpful when the same issue appears in several files. It also lets you prepare a short, relevant packet for an advocate or meeting without forwarding an entire archive. If several caregivers help, agree on who adds official documents and how corrections are labeled. Avoid editing the only copy of a school report to insert your comments. Your observations deserve a place where their authorship and date are clear. Keep a small decision and question log+After a meeting or important call, record the date, participants, what you understood, and what still needs confirmation. Label your own notes as your notes. An unanswered email or uncorrected summary does not automatically turn your understanding into the school's agreement. Store important email threads with their dates and attachments. If you print them, check that the sender and subject remain visible. You rarely need every routine reminder; keep records that help explain decisions, requests, progress, or a significant concern. Protect access as carefully as you organize it+Use secure storage, individual accounts where possible, and a sensible backup. Check who can open a shared link before sending it. Share the smallest relevant set through an appropriate school or professional channel, and review access when a working relationship ends. Avoid putting IEPs, student photographs, assessment reports, or personal-care details into public sites or unapproved tools. A helpful template can be shared publicly with blank fields; a completed student record belongs in a private, appropriate channel. If documents are missing, request them. Under IDEA, parents have rights to inspect and review relevant education records without unnecessary delay and before specified meetings or proceedings, with an outside limit of 45 days. The rule also covers reasonable requests for explanation and certain access-related copies; state rules may add protections. Read IDEA's records-access provision.
